title: Measuring size from a reference marker
summary: Turn pixels into millimeters with a card or ArUco marker: why one photo has no scale, why a pixels-per-mm ratio fails under tilt, how a homography rectifies the plane, and how big each error source really is.
outcomes: Explain with similar triangles why pixel size depends on depth and why a reference must share the object's plane
Compute an object's length by mapping its endpoint pixels through a card-to-millimeter homography
Explain why a single pixels-per-mm ratio fails on a tilted photo and estimate how wrong it is
Describe what ArUco detection, camera calibration and solvePnP each provide and when you need them
Estimate the error from corner noise, lens distortion and an object that sits above the reference plane

lessons.title: Why a photo has no scale until you add a reference

blocks.md:
A phone app wants to say "this bolt is 70 mm long" from one photo. The photo only contains pixels. Whether 100 pixels is 10 mm or 10 m depends on how far away the thing was, and a single image does not record that distance.

The standard fix is to put an object of **known size** next to the thing you measure: a printed fiducial marker, a coin, or a bank card. This course works out exactly when that trick is valid, how to do it properly, and how large the errors are.

The **pinhole camera model** treats the camera as a single point (the optical center) and an image plane. A 3D point at camera coordinates $(X, Y, Z)$, with $Z$ the depth along the viewing axis, lands at pixel $u = f_x X / Z + c_x$, $v = f_y Y / Z + c_y$. Here $f_x, f_y$ are the **focal lengths in pixel units** and $(c_x, c_y)$ is the **principal point**, usually near the image center. These four numbers are the camera's **intrinsics**.

blocks.caption: Similar triangles: an object of fixed physical size shrinks in the image in proportion to 1/Z, its distance from the camera.

blocks.md: A tiny example. Take $f = 1000$ px and an ID-1 card, the format of bank cards defined by ISO/IEC 7810, which is **85.60 mm by 53.98 mm**. Held face-on at $Z = 400$ mm, its width spans $1000 \cdot 85.6 / 400 = 214$ px. Move it to 420 mm and it spans 203.8 px; at 380 mm it spans 225.3 px. A 5 percent change in depth is a 5 percent change in apparent size.

blocks.title: Card width in pixels versus distance

scenes.caption: With f = 1000 px the card's 85.6 mm side spans 214 px at 400 mm. The curve is a hyperbola: pixel size falls as 1/Z.
At 420 mm the same card spans only 203.8 px. Nothing in the pixels says whether the card shrank or moved away.
A longer focal length (zooming in) scales every pixel size up, so even f must be known or cancelled out.
The fix: the pixels-to-mm conversion is measured from a reference at the same depth as the object, so both Z and f cancel.

blocks.md:
This is why a reference works: if the object sits at the same depth as the card, both are scaled by the same $f/Z$, and the ratio of their pixel sizes equals the ratio of their real sizes. You never need to know $f$ or $Z$.

It is also why the reference must be **in the object's plane**. An object 20 mm closer to the camera than the card is magnified by a different factor, and no amount of math on the card can tell you that.
A reference object gives you scale only for points at its depth (more precisely, on its plane). Everything else in the image has a different pixels-per-mm.

blocks.question: A coin of known diameter lies on a table next to a mug. You photograph them from above and compute mm per pixel from the coin, then measure the mug's rim diameter. What goes wrong?
options: Nothing, because the coin and the rim are in the same photo and share one scale
The rim is closer to the camera than the coin, so it looks larger and the measurement overestimates it
The rim is farther from the camera, so the measurement underestimates it
The coin is round, so it cannot give a scale at all
blocks.explain: The mug's rim sits a mug's height above the table, so its depth Z is smaller and its magnification f/Z is larger. The coin's scale is valid only on the table plane, so the rim reads too large.

lessons.title: Why one pixels-per-mm ratio fails on a tilted photo

blocks.md:
The simplest method: measure the card's width in pixels, divide by 85.60 to get a **pixels-per-mm ratio**, and divide every other pixel length by it. This is exact when the camera looks straight down at the table, because then every point on the table has the same depth.

Real phone photos are taken at an angle. Here is the toy scene used for the rest of the course.

**Toy scene** (simplified: a synthetic pinhole camera with $f = 1000$ px, principal point (640, 360), no lens distortion). A card lies on a table. The camera looks at a point 400 mm away, tilted 40 degrees from straight down. Projected corners, rounded to whole pixels as a detector without sub-pixel refinement would report them, in the order top-left, top-right, bottom-right, bottom-left:

- TL (459, 316), TR (666, 316), BR (668, 420), BL (443, 420)

A bolt lies on the table beside the card. Its true length is **70 mm**. Its endpoints are at pixels (706, 420) and (801, 312), which are 143.84 px apart.

blocks.title: Pixels per mm along each edge of the tilted card

scenes.caption: The card is a rectangle, but in the image it is a trapezoid: the top edge is 207 px, the bottom edge 225 px.
The top edge is farther away (depth 415 mm versus 381 mm for the bottom). 381/415 = 0.92, which matches 207/225 = 0.92: plain 1/Z scaling.
Along the tilted direction the card is also foreshortened: about 1.95 px per mm, versus 2.42 to 2.63 across. The scale depends on direction too.
So there is no single pixels-per-mm ratio. Which one should the bolt use? It lies beside the card, partly along the tilted direction.

blocks.prompt: Using the top edge ratio (207 / 85.60 = 2.42 px per mm), what length does the naive method give for the bolt, whose image is 143.84 px long? Guess whether it lands above or below 70 mm, and by roughly how much.
blocks.reveal: It gives 143.84 / 2.418 = **59.5 mm**, 15 percent short. The bottom edge ratio gives 54.7 mm and the average of the two gives 57.0 mm. All are too small, because the bolt runs partly along the tilted direction, where each millimeter covers fewer pixels than along the card's width. Averaging edges cannot fix a direction-dependent scale.

blocks.title: Bolt length by method (true length 70 mm)

scenes.caption: Ground truth: the bolt is 70 mm long.
Naive ratios give 59.5, 54.7 and 57.0 mm. The error comes from perspective, not from noise, so it does not average away.
Next lesson: mapping the bolt's endpoints through a homography fitted to the 4 card corners gives 69.95 mm, even with corners rounded to whole pixels.

blocks.md: A common misconception is that the pixels-per-mm method only fails at extreme angles. In this toy, a moderate 40 degree tilt already puts it 15 percent off. Under perspective, scale varies with both position and direction across the plane.

blocks.question: When is a single pixels-per-mm ratio from the card exact for an object on the same table?
options: Whenever the card and the object are both fully visible
When you average the ratios from all four edges
When the image plane is parallel to the table, so every table point has the same depth
When the object is shorter than the card
blocks.explain: With the camera looking straight at the plane, every point on it has the same Z, so f/Z is one constant. Averaging edges or keeping the object short reduces nothing about perspective; only a fronto-parallel view makes the ratio constant (ignoring lens distortion).

lessons.title: Rectifying the plane: card corners to millimeters

blocks.md:
Recall from the previous course: a **homography** is a 3x3 matrix $H$ that maps points between two planes, and the DLT (direct linear transform) fits it from at least 4 point correspondences. Each correspondence gives 2 linear equations and $H$ has 8 degrees of freedom (9 entries, up to scale), so 4 points in general position determine it exactly.

The image of a flat table is a homography of the table itself. So we can map pixels **to table millimeters** directly.

blocks.tex: \begin{bmatrix} x' \\ y' \\ w \end{bmatrix} = H \begin{bmatrix} u \\ v \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad (x, y)_{\text{mm}} = \left( \frac{x'}{w}, \frac{y'}{w} \right)
blocks.caption: A pixel (u, v) in homogeneous form is multiplied by H, then divided by the third coordinate w. The division is what undoes perspective.

scenes.caption: Each detected corner pixel is paired with where that corner really is on the card, in millimeters, with the origin at the bottom-left corner.
The card's known size supplies the right-hand side. This is the only physical knowledge the method uses: 85.60 by 53.98 mm.
4 pairs give 8 equations for H's 8 unknowns. The fitted H maps all four corners back exactly to their mm positions.

blocks.md:
Fitting the DLT to the rounded corners gives (rounded for display)

$H \approx \begin{bmatrix} 0.5620 & 0.0865 & -285.29 \\ 0 & -0.7054 & 296.28 \\ 0 & 0.001136 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$

The bottom row is what makes this a perspective map rather than an affine one: $w$ grows with $v$, so points lower in the image (closer to the camera) get divided by more.

scenes.caption: Map the first endpoint, pixel (706, 420). Before dividing, the homogeneous result is (147.81, 0.00, 1.4773).
Dividing by w gives the point on the table: (100.06, 0.00) mm. The true endpoint was (100, 0), off by 0.06 mm due to rounding.
The second endpoint, pixel (801, 312), is higher in the image and farther away: its w is smaller (1.3545), so it gets stretched more.
b = (141.65, 56.24) mm. The distance on the rectified plane is 69.95 mm against a true 70 mm.

blocks.code:
import cv2, numpy as np

img_pts = np.float32([[459, 316], [666, 316], [668, 420], [443, 420]])  # TL, TR, BR, BL
mm_pts = np.float32([[0, 53.98], [85.6, 53.98], [85.6, 0], [0, 0]])
H = cv2.getPerspectiveTransform(img_pts, mm_pts)

ends = np.float32([[[706, 420]], [[801, 312]]])
a, b = cv2.perspectiveTransform(ends, H)[:, 0]
print(np.linalg.norm(b - a))  # about 69.95 mm

# Optional: a top-down view at 4 px per mm, for drawing or clicking
top = cv2.warpPerspective(img, np.diag([4, 4, 1]) @ H, (800, 400))
blocks.caption: The same computation in OpenCV. getPerspectiveTransform solves for H from exactly 4 pairs; findHomography accepts more points and robust fitting. Note: in a top-down warp, image y points down, so you may want to flip the mm y axis.

blocks.md: Map the object's **points** into plane millimeters first, then measure there. Never measure in pixels and convert with a scalar; the homography's division by w is where perspective gets removed.

blocks.question: A colleague fits H from the card corners, but lists the mm points in the order TL, BL, BR, TR while the pixel points are TL, TR, BR, BL. What happens?
options: H maps the card onto a transposed card, so lengths along the card's width and height are swapped and measurements are wrong
OpenCV automatically sorts the points, so nothing changes
The fit fails with an error because the points are not in clockwise order
Only the sign of the result flips
blocks.explain: The solver trusts the pairing you give it. Swapped pairs still define a valid homography, just to a wrong rectangle (85.6 placed along the 53.98 side), so it returns confidently wrong numbers. This is why ArUco returns corners in a fixed order.

lessons.title: ArUco markers, camera calibration and solvePnP

blocks.md:
A card works, but finding its corners is fragile: ID-1 corners are rounded (radius 2.88 to 3.48 mm per ISO/IEC 7810), so you must fit lines to the edges and intersect them, and cards come in many colors.

**ArUco markers** are designed for this. Per the OpenCV tutorial, a marker is a square with a wide black border and an inner binary grid that encodes an ID; a 4x4 marker carries 16 bits. A single marker gives four corner correspondences, enough for a homography or a camera pose. The library comes from Rafael Muñoz and Sergio Garrido (Garrido-Jurado et al., 2014).

blocks.title: From photo to measurement with a marker

scenes.caption: Detection first finds square-looking contours (after adaptive thresholding) and discards shapes that are not convex quadrilaterals.
For each candidate, the perspective is removed, the cells are thresholded (Otsu) into bits, and the bits are matched against a dictionary, with error correction.
Output: the ID and the four corners in a fixed order, clockwise from top-left. A known order means no corner-pairing bugs.
For measuring things lying on the marker's plane, a homography from the corners to mm is enough. No calibration needed if lens distortion is small.
To get the marker's 3D pose, or to correct a distorting lens, you need intrinsics K and distortion coefficients from a one-time calibration.

blocks.md:
**Calibration.** OpenCV's `calibrateCamera` estimates the intrinsic matrix $K$ (the docs call it $A$, following Zhang's 2000 paper) and distortion coefficients from many views of a planar pattern such as a chessboard. Its initialization works only for planar patterns, then a Levenberg-Marquardt optimization minimizes **reprojection error**, the squared pixel distance between detected and predicted pattern points. The tutorial suggests at least 10 views; the API docs recommend views with strong tilt over a range of distances.

The ArUco tutorial notes this needs doing once, unless the optics change, for instance a change of focus.

blocks.caption: OpenCV's distortion model in normalized coordinates (x = X/Z, r^2 = x^2 + y^2): radial terms k1, k2, k3 bend straight lines, more so far from the center; tangential terms p1, p2 come from a lens not parallel to the sensor. y is analogous.

blocks.title: Radial distortion shift versus distance from center

scenes.caption: With only k1 = -0.1 (barrel-type, illustrative value) and f = 1000 px, a point 200 px from center moves 0.8 px; at 400 px it moves 6.4 px.
At 600 px from center the shift is 21.6 px. Shift grows as r cubed, so a marker near the image edge is far more distorted than one in the middle.
Distortion is not a homography: it bends straight card edges. Undistort first (cv.undistort or undistortPoints), then fit H.

blocks.md: **Pose.** With $K$ and distortion known, `cv::solvePnP` finds the rotation and translation (rvec, tvec) that best project known 3D points onto the detected pixels. For a single square marker, the flag `SOLVEPNP_IPPE_SQUARE` is a special case for marker pose: exactly 4 object points ordered $(-s/2, s/2, 0), (s/2, s/2, 0), (s/2, -s/2, 0), (-s/2, -s/2, 0)$, where $s$ is the side length. The ArUco tutorial stresses that tvec comes out **in the units you gave for the marker side**.

blocks.prompt: You print a marker whose black square is 50 mm wide, but pass markerLength = 0.05 to the pose code. The camera is about 400 mm from the marker. What does tvec's length come out as?
blocks.reveal: About **0.4**, in meters, because the pose is in the same units as the marker side. Passing 50 would give about 400 (mm). Both are correct; the bug happens when one part of a pipeline assumes mm and another meters. Also note the side length is the black square, not the paper including the white margin.

blocks.question: You only need to measure flat objects lying next to a marker, and your lens has negligible distortion near the image center. What is the minimum you need?
options: A full calibration with 10 or more chessboard views, then solvePnP
The marker's 4 detected corners and its physical side length, then a homography to mm
The camera's focal length from the phone's EXIF data, then similar triangles
Two photos from different positions for stereo depth
blocks.explain: For points on the marker's plane, the plane-to-image map is a homography and the 4 corners plus the known side length determine it. Intrinsics enter only when you need 3D pose or must remove lens distortion. A focal length alone does not give Z.

blocks.question: After calibrating a phone camera, the app lets the camera autofocus between shots. Why might measurements drift?
options: Autofocus changes the ArUco dictionary
Autofocus re-orders the detected corners
Refocusing has no effect on geometry, so they should not drift
Refocusing changes the optics, so the calibrated intrinsics and distortion may no longer match
blocks.explain: The OpenCV ArUco tutorial says calibration is valid unless the camera optics are modified, giving a change of focus as the example. A homography-only pipeline is less affected because it refits H from the marker in every photo, but undistortion still uses the stored coefficients.

lessons.title: How wrong is it? Corner noise, out-of-plane height, pixels

blocks.md:
With the method in place, the remaining question is precision. Four error sources dominate:

1. **Corner localization**: each corner pixel is a bit off, and H inherits that.
2. **Pixel quantization**: endpoints and corners are read on a grid.
3. **Lens distortion**: covered in the previous lesson; undistort first.
4. **Out-of-plane geometry**: the object is not on the reference plane.

We size each one on the toy scene.

blocks.prompt: Move just one card corner by 1 pixel and refit H. The bolt is 70 mm, and the card spans about 210 px. How much do you expect the bolt's measured length to change: about 0.05 mm, about 0.3 mm, or more than 1 mm?
blocks.reveal: Up to **1.28 mm** (1.8 percent), when the top-right corner moves 1 px down: the bolt then reads 71.23 mm. A 1 px move of the same corner up gives 68.71 mm. The card is small in the image, so 1 px is a large fraction of its size, and the bolt lies outside the card, so the error is extrapolated.

blocks.title: Worst bolt-length change from a 1 px shift of one corner

scenes.caption: Worst case over 4 shift directions (up, down, left, right) for each corner, bolt outside the card. TR matters most: the bolt's far end (142, 56) lies beyond the card's top-right corner, so H is extrapolated past it.
The same test for a 70 mm segment centered on the card along its diagonal: at most 0.24 mm, about 5 times smaller. Interpolating within the reference is much safer than extrapolating.

blocks.md:
A Monte Carlo check with independent Gaussian noise of 0.5 px on every corner coordinate (20,000 trials) gives a bolt length of 69.96 mm with a standard deviation of **0.93 mm**. Sub-pixel corner refinement matters: OpenCV offers `cornerSubPix` for chessboards and `cornerRefinementMethod` in the ArUco detector parameters.

**Quantization.** Near the bolt one pixel covers 0.38 to 0.57 mm of table, depending on direction and position. Rounding the bolt's endpoints alone moves the result from 70.02 to 69.95 mm here.

**Out of plane.** A homography is only correct for points on the card's plane. Suppose the camera looks straight down from $Z = 400$ mm and the thing you measure is a top surface $h = 20$ mm above the table, like the top of a box. That surface is at depth $Z - h = 380$ mm, so it is magnified by $f/380$ while the homography assumes $f/400$.

blocks.caption: Similar triangles, head-on case: the raised edge projects to the same pixels as a longer segment on the table.

blocks.title: Out-of-plane error versus height above the reference

scenes.caption: At Z = 400 mm, an object 20 mm above the plane reads 5.3 percent long: 73.68 mm for a true 70 mm. That is nearly 3 times the worst 1 px corner error (1.28 mm).
Errors grow fast: 10 mm gives 2.6 percent, 40 mm gives 11.1 percent at the same distance.
Moving the camera back to 1000 mm shrinks the 20 mm case to about 2 percent, but the marker gets smaller in the image, which raises the corner-noise error.

blocks.md: In the tilted toy scene, lifting the bolt 20 mm (keeping its plan position) makes it read **74.89 mm**, 7.0 percent long: with an oblique camera, height also shifts the apparent position on the plane, so the error depends on where and how the object sits. The head-on formula is a useful rule of thumb, not an exact bound.

Practical recipe: put the marker on the same surface as the edges you measure, close to the object, and as large in the frame as you can. Shoot roughly head-on, near the image center. Use sub-pixel corners, undistort if the lens is wide, and validate against a ruler. For tall objects, measure the base, or put the marker at the height you care about.

blocks.question: A fish lies on a dock and you place a marker beside it. The fish's back is about 30 mm above the dock and the phone is 500 mm away, held head-on. Measuring nose to tail along the outline seen from above, roughly how far off might you be?
options: Under 0.5 percent, because the marker corrects perspective
About 2 percent short, because raised parts look smaller
Up to about 6 percent long for points at the back's height, since 30 / (500 - 30) is about 6.4 percent
About 30 percent long, equal to the ratio of heights
blocks.explain: The homography is valid only on the dock plane. Points 30 mm up are magnified by 500/470, about 6.4 percent. Nose and tail are probably closer to the dock than the back, so the real error is somewhere between 0 and that bound.

blocks.question: Your measured lengths have about 1 mm of scatter between photos. Which change most directly reduces corner-noise error?
options: Switch from a homography to the pixels-per-mm ratio
Print a larger marker and place the object within or close to its footprint
Increase JPEG compression to reduce noise
Use a marker dictionary with more IDs
blocks.explain: A 1 px corner error is a smaller fraction of a larger marker, and objects inside the reference footprint are interpolated, not extrapolated (0.24 mm versus 1.28 mm in the toy). Dictionary size affects ID confusion, not corner accuracy.
